newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's EPS, Czech Skoda sign $62 mln power deal.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's EPS, Czech Skoda sign $62 mln power deal.

text.p: Serbia's power company Elektroprivreda Srbije (EPS) and Czech engineering concern Skoda a.s. signed a $62 million commercial deal on Tuesday as part of a project to equip the Kolubara B thermal power plant.
The deal will become operational once the two sides finalise details over financing.

A Yugoslav bank consortium, consisting of Beogradska banka, Vojvodjanska banka, Investbanka and Jugobanka Beograd, has agreed with Czech Obchodni Banka a.s. to prepare the ground for EPS and the Czech bank to sign a credit deal by June 15, 1997.

"The Serbian government has given EPS approval to conclude an agreement on a credit with the Czech Obchodni bank amounting to $100 million," EPS General Manager Slobodan Babic said at a signing ceremony in the Serbian Chamber of Commerce.
"Once concluded, the credit will bring the contracts signed today into a stage of realisation," Babic said.
The present value of commercial contracts is $62 million while the remaining $38 million will be concluded by the end of the year, Babic added.

Under the deal, the two sides will work together on the building and equipping of two 350 megawatt coal burning blocks at the Kolubara B thermal power plant, one to be completed by the year 2000 and the second by 2001.
"A lot of work preceded this signing," Babic said referring to more than 18 months of negotiations with Skoda.
The Kolubara B project began in 1985 but was discontinued in 1992 when war-related international sanctions were imposed on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro.
The Serbian government has given completion of the 700-megawatt Kolubara B plant priority in its medium-term energy development strategy.
With the break-up of the former Yugoslav federation, EPS was forced to look for partners elsewhere.
"And one of these partners is Skoda concern," said Dragan Kostic, president of EPS Board of Directors.
The main Yugoslav sub-contractors will be Minel, Gosa, MIN and Mostogradnja.
The deal will be Serbia's first major credit arrangement since sanctions were lifted in October last year.

"We began cooperation three years ago in a time which was to say the least strange. But even in those hard times, we found means to cooperate," said Skoda concern president and Managing Director Lubomir Soudek.
"The meetings we had with the Yugoslav side in that period were 'half-secret' and I am glad to say we can now cooperate publicly," said Soudek, who signed the contracts for Skoda.

"We are pleased that EPS' partner is Skoda concern which proved that during transition and restructuring large capacities from previous systems can be organised in a modern way and compete equally in market conditions," said Serbia's Deputy Prime Minister Svetozar Krstic.
Yugoslavia and the Czech Republic signed an accord on trade cooperation in September 1996, less than a year after sanctions were suspended.
Kostic said the entire Kolubara B project is much bigger and requires engagement of other sub-contractors.
"What we signed today is a commercial contract for several components -- two generators, the main hall and metal construction for building the hall," Kostic told Reuters.
According to him, other works would be subject to separate agreements.

"The $100 million dollars is a large sum for our country in a time like this. The project is important because it partially employs local industry and because such projects lend direct support to Yugoslavia's reform programmes," Yugoslav Deputy Prime Minister Danko Djunic told Reuters. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305
